2. The petitioner filed an application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) in the Court of Munsif 3rd Court, Comilla for preemption alleging, inter alia, that the opposite party was a stranger purchaser in respect of the land in question while the petitioner was a co-sharer tenant of the holding. The said miscellaneous case was allowed exparte on 7.3.75. Thereupon the opposite-party filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the exparte order on 15.5.75 alleging, besides other things, non-service and fraudulent suppression of notice of the preemption case. 

 3. The learned Munsif, however, dismissed the said application upon the findings that the notice was served upon the opposites party and the application was barred by limitation. An appeal having been taken against the said order of the learned Munsif, the learned Subordinate judge as already stated, reversed the order of the learned Munsif and restored the pre-emption case. The learned Subordinate judge found that no notice was served upon the opposite party and the petition also was not barred by limitation. 

 5. Mr. Syed Habibul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite-party has contended that the exparte order passed by the learned Munsif in the pre-emption case allowing the application for preemption should be regarded as a decree as it was an adjudication conclusively determining the rights of the parties in the proceeding. If it could be so held then obviously an appeal lay under Order 43 rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his Contention he has cited two decisions reported in A.I.R. 1928 Mad 969 (Selvarayan Samson vs. S. Amalorpavanadam) and 1948 Mad, 416 (Krishna Uddayan vs. Chinna Pillai). Next, Mr. Huq has read out certain statements from the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the opposite-party and submitted on the basis thereof that the application of the petitioner under section 96 of the Act was barred by limitation and fraud was practised by him in suppressing the court's process. The appellate court also found that notice was not served. In such circumstances, he has prayed that this Court should not exercise its discretionary jurisdiction and interfere with the order of the learned Subordinate Judge which according to him, serves the interest of justice although the appeal itself may be held to be incompetent, in this connection he has referred to the principle laid down in the case of Srinibash Mukhopadhya and another vs. Elahi Malder and others 10 D.L.R. 522. 

 In the case of Krishna Udayan vs. Chinna Pillai A.I.R. 1958 Madras 416, a learned Single Judge held that an appeal lay under Order 43 rule 1(d) C.P.C. from an order passed under Order 9 rule 13 rejecting an application to set aside an exparte order passed under section 30 of Land Acquisition Act. 

 7. The reason given was that section 53 of the Land Acquisition Act made the provisions of C.P.C. applicable to all proceedings before the court under that Act save in so far as they are not inconsistent with any provision of Land Acquisition Act and since there was nothing inconsistent between the provisions of Land Acquisition Act and those of Order 9 rule 13 and Order 43 rule 1(d) C.P.C. the appeal was held to be competent. 

 8. At another place, it was held that the ex-parte order passed by the subordinate Judge under section 30 of Land Acquisition Act was a decree having relied upon a Full Bench decision of the said Court to the effect that a Judge appointed to decide a dispute referred under section 30 of the said Act was a Civil Court and the decision therein was a decree. 

 9. It is clear that in that case the provisions of Land Acquisition Act and an order under that Act were the subject matter for consideration. But in the case before us, we have a different statute and an exparte order made thereunder. The question involved in this case was directly in issue in the case reported in 4 D. L.R. 621 which we shall presently examine. 

 12. In so far as the submission of Mr. Haque the learned Advocate, to the fact that the exparte order passed in the application under Order 9 rule 13 should be treated as decree, is concerned, it may be pointed out that Ibrahim, J. in the aforesaid decision negatived the said contention by analysing the scheme of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The reasoning given therein is equally applicable to an order passed under section 96 of the Act. 13. We would like to add yet another reason as to the difficulty in construing an order under section 96 of the Act to be a decree.
